paragraphs: EMDiffusion addresses a practical obstacle in using diffusion models for image reconstruction: learning useful image structure usually requires many clean training images. In settings where observations are already corrupted, that requirement limits the models’ usefulness. The paper proposes learning a clean-image distribution through an iterative process that works from the corrupted observations.

The method alternates two connected operations using expectation-maximization. In the expectation step, an available diffusion model helps reconstruct clean images from the observations. In the maximization step, those reconstructions become the basis for updating the diffusion model’s weights. The updated model can then support the next reconstruction step, linking improvements in reconstruction and model learning.

The abstract describes this process as gradually converging to a local optimum that approximates the clean-data distribution. That qualification matters: the stated result is local convergence, rather than guaranteed recovery of the exact distribution. Experiments cover random inpainting, denoising, and deblurring, with reported state-of-the-art performance. These results support the approach’s usefulness across several forms of computational imaging corruption.
neurips-2024-an-expectation-maximization.tldr: EMDiffusion alternates image reconstruction and diffusion-model updates to learn an approximation of clean image data from corrupted observations.

paragraphs: This paper examines how feasibly an attacker can reconstruct a neural network’s parameters with high numerical fidelity. Earlier cryptanalytic methods had recovered parameters for small networks trained on random data, but their computational expense raised questions about applicability to networks trained on standard benchmarks. The study revisits those methods in that more practical setting.

The authors combine earlier attacks into a unified codebase and show that computational tools substantially affect performance. They also improve the overall attack, including a procedure that distinguishes neurons whose weight signs are easier or harder to recover. This accelerates sign extraction by up to 14.8 times. Their analysis identifies weight extraction itself, rather than sign extraction, as the main bottleneck.

With these improvements, they extract a two-hidden-layer MNIST model containing 16,721 parameters in 98 minutes, compared with at least 150 minutes previously. This is a concrete feasibility result for the studied model. The paper also proposes more robust benchmarking methods to address methodological weaknesses in previous extraction studies and make future comparisons more informative.
neurips-2024-beyond-slow-signs-in-high-f.tldr: An improved model-extraction implementation speeds parameter recovery and identifies weight extraction, rather than sign recovery, as the central bottleneck.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to incorporate information about a graph’s overall topology into a graph neural network. Persistent homology provides such information, but the authors report that simply adding its features to network layers brings only marginal improvements and offers limited interpretability. They instead focus on pooling, the operation that produces a coarser graph for subsequent processing.

Their key observation is that the filtration operation used in persistent homology naturally aligns with graph pooling through a cutoff mechanism. They build on this connection to inject global topological invariance directly into pooling layers. Consequently, later message passing follows a pooled topology informed by persistence, making the topological information part of the graph structure on which computation proceeds.

The authors apply this mechanism to a collection of existing graph pooling methods. Across several popular datasets, they report consistent and substantial performance improvements. These experiments support the mechanism’s flexibility across the tested pooling approaches. The contribution is therefore a way of integrating topology into graph reduction, with evidence that this integration improves downstream network performance.
neurips-2024-boosting-graph-pooling-with.tldr: Integrating persistent homology directly into graph pooling produces topology-informed coarse graphs and improves performance across tested pooling methods.

paragraphs: DEFT tackles conditional generation using an existing, expensive-to-train unconditional diffusion model. In an inverse problem, generation must account for an observation or constraint. The paper argues that many approaches to this task lack a shared mathematical framework, making their relationships difficult to understand and contributing to practical difficulties involving tuning, training expense, or access to model weights.

The authors use Doob’s h-transform to place conditional training and sampling within one framework. This perspective motivates a concrete method: train a very small network to learn the conditional transformation while leaving the large unconditional network unchanged. The additional network supplies the learned conditioning component, allowing the approach to build on an existing generative model.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results across linear and nonlinear benchmarks, with image-reconstruction speedups reaching 1.6 times. It also reports the best perceptual quality on natural images and reconstruction performance on medical images among the evaluated approaches. Initial protein motif scaffolding experiments outperform reconstruction guidance methods, providing preliminary evidence beyond image reconstruction.
neurips-2024-deft-efficient-fine-tuning-.tldr: DEFT learns a small conditioning network through Doob’s h-transform while keeping a large diffusion model fixed, improving speed and reconstruction results.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes diffusion generation as a connected training-and-sampling process. Much previous theory starts by assuming that the model’s score function has already reached a specified accuracy, then studies how that error affects generation. The authors instead examine how training produces the score estimate and how its quality interacts with the subsequent sampling procedure.

They provide a non-asymptotic convergence analysis of denoising score matching trained with gradient descent. This addresses learning at finite training scales rather than only its limiting behavior. They combine it with a refined sampling-error analysis for variance-exploding diffusion models. Together, these results account for errors arising in both stages and give theoretical guidance for their design.

The analysis favors training noise distributions and loss weighting that qualitatively agree with choices described in earlier work. It also makes the preferred sampling schedule depend on score quality: one existing design is preferable when the score is well trained, while another becomes preferable when it is less trained. The implication is conditional guidance, connecting sampling choices to the quality achieved during training.
neurips-2024-evaluating-the-design-space.tldr: A joint analysis of diffusion training and sampling shows how suitable generation choices depend on the accuracy of the learned score.

paragraphs: Graph alignment seeks a correspondence between two graphs that makes their structures as similar as possible under a chosen distance measure. This problem arises in settings including biology, chemistry, recommendations, and social networks. Finding the desired alignment is computationally difficult: the underlying optimization problem is NP-hard, motivating methods that simplify the space in which they search.

Many existing approaches work through intermediate representations such as embeddings, spectra, or graph signals. The paper argues that restricting alignment to these spaces can distort the original problem and miss high-quality matches. FUGAL instead operates directly on the graphs’ adjacency matrices. It uses carefully chosen constraint relaxation to find a permutation matrix representing the mapping between the graphs.

Across the benchmark datasets studied, the authors report that FUGAL consistently improves alignment accuracy over state-of-the-art methods without compromising efficiency. These findings support direct adjacency-based optimization as a practical approach in the evaluated settings. The central contribution is the combination of working with the original graph structure and relaxing constraints to make that optimization tractable.
neurips-2024-fugal-feature-fortified-unr.tldr: FUGAL aligns graphs directly through their adjacency matrices, reporting improved matching accuracy without sacrificing efficiency on the tested benchmarks.

paragraphs: Single-cell RNA sequencing measures gene expression across individual cells, but its data can contain noisy values and false zeros. These errors can interfere with identifying cell groups or recovering expression patterns. Existing propagation-based imputation methods use nearest-neighbor graphs to fill in missing signal, yet the paper argues that their gene-relationship modeling is incomplete.

The proposed method incorporates both associating and dissociating relationships between genes, following the genetic evidence described by the authors. It constructs an additional nearest-neighbor graph using the negated cell-by-gene matrix to capture dissociating relationships. It also standardizes each gene’s value distribution in terms of mean and variance, placing different genes on a common distributional footing for the method.

Experiments across six single-cell RNA sequencing datasets evaluate both cell clustering and gene-expression recovery. The authors report substantial gains over state-of-the-art methods on these tasks. The findings support the value of modeling dissociating relationships alongside associating ones when repairing these data. Their significance extends beyond filling matrix entries: improved imputation also benefits the tested downstream grouping of cells.
neurips-2024-gene-gene-relationship-mode.tldr: Modeling both associating and dissociating gene relationships improves single-cell expression imputation and cell clustering across six tested datasets.

paragraphs: Deep Image Prior reconstructs an image from noisy measurements and a forward operator without requiring a training dataset. It uses a randomly initialized deep network to learn the image’s structure during reconstruction. However, the network’s many parameters also make it vulnerable to fitting measurement noise, weakening its usefulness as reconstruction continues.

Autoencoding Sequential Deep Image Prior, or aSeqDIP, addresses this problem through progressive denoising and reconstruction. Inspired by gradual denoising in diffusion models, it sequentially optimizes network weights using an objective that adapts to the input. An additional autoencoding regularization term forms part of this objective. The method thus changes how reconstruction proceeds while preserving the ability to work without training data.

The authors report better mitigation of noise overfitting than other DIP-based methods, using a similar number of parameter updates to vanilla DIP. They evaluate the approach on MRI and CT reconstruction, as well as denoising, inpainting, and nonlinear deblurring. These results support the sequential approach across several reconstruction and restoration tasks, with the reported computational comparison specifically concerning parameter-update counts.
neurips-2024-image-reconstruction-via-au.tldr: aSeqDIP progressively reconstructs images without training data while reducing noise overfitting at a parameter-update count similar to vanilla Deep Image Prior.

paragraphs: Concept Bottleneck Models connect predictions to concepts that people can understand and potentially modify. However, understandable inputs to a decision do not automatically make the decision process fully interpretable. This paper addresses the remaining opacity in the task predictor, which the authors identify as an obstacle to inspecting and formally verifying its behavior before deployment.

The Concept-based Memory Reasoner represents each prediction through two stages. A neural mechanism first selects a rule from a memory of learnable logical rules. The selected rule is then evaluated symbolically. This explicit memory exposes rules for expert inspection, while symbolic evaluation supports formal verification of certain global properties relevant to the task’s prediction process.

Experiments show a better accuracy–interpretability trade-off than state-of-the-art Concept Bottleneck Models. The model also discovers rules consistent with ground truths and permits rule interventions and verification before deployment. The contribution is an architecture that makes the rule-based prediction process inspectable and supports checking specified properties; the abstract’s verification claim concerns those properties rather than an unrestricted guarantee about every aspect of the system.
neurips-2024-interpretable-concept-based.tldr: A memory of learned logical rules makes concept-based predictions inspectable, editable, and amenable to formal verification of specified properties.

paragraphs: This paper develops fast algorithms for approximating invariant subspaces in generalized eigenvalue problems. These subspaces underpin tasks such as principal component analysis and electronic-structure calculations. The goal is to compute an approximate spectral projector: a matrix representing the subspace associated with a chosen number of the smallest or largest eigenvalues.

The result applies to Hermitian matrices H and S, with S positive-definite. It bounds the projector’s spectral-norm error by a requested tolerance, with success probability 1 minus 1/n. The bit-operation cost is close to the matrix-multiplication exponent, with additional polylogarithmic dependence on matrix size, inverse accuracy, the conditioning of S, and the inverse gap between the relevant neighboring eigenvalues.

To establish this numerical guarantee, the authors develop a stability analysis for Cholesky factorization and a smoothed analysis for computing spectral gaps. These ingredients explicitly support control of error in the computed projector. The resulting complexity bounds extend to classical PCA and randomized low-rank approximation, providing theoretical guarantees for both computational cost and approximation accuracy.
neurips-2024-invariant-subspaces-and-pca.tldr: New numerical analyses enable provably accurate invariant-subspace and PCA computations with bit complexity close to matrix multiplication.

paragraphs: Vision transformers can accept different sequence lengths, yet often struggle when a larger test image produces more patches than they encountered during training. This paper attributes that difficulty to positional encodings that create a distribution shift at higher resolutions. LookHere replaces the positional encoding of plain vision transformers to improve this form of extrapolation.

The method uses two-dimensional attention masks to give attention heads fixed fields of view pointing in different directions. This design provides translation equivariance, ensures diversity among heads, and limits the distribution shift they experience when the number of patches grows. Spatial organization is therefore expressed through directed attention patterns that remain useful across image sizes.

On ImageNet without extrapolation, the authors report average improvements of 1.6% in classification and 5.4% against adversarial attack, plus a 1.5% decrease in calibration error. When training at 224 by 224 pixels and testing at 1024 by 1024, LookHere outperforms 2D-RoPE by 21.7%. The paper also introduces ImageNet-HR to support evaluation of high-resolution image classifiers.
neurips-2024-lookhere-vision-transformer.tldr: LookHere uses directed attention masks to improve vision-transformer performance and extrapolation to images larger than those used in training.

paragraphs: Make-An-Agent explores generating a control policy from demonstrations of desired behavior. The output is a policy network that can govern an agent’s actions. The paper frames this as behavior-to-policy generation, using a conditional diffusion model to produce the parameters needed for a policy rather than requiring a separate conventional policy-learning process for each demonstrated behavior.

The generator is trained on policy-network checkpoints paired with their corresponding trajectories. It converts trajectory information into behavior embeddings, which guide generation of latent parameter representations. Those representations are decoded into policy networks. This connects examples of behavior to the underlying network parameters that can produce an agent’s decisions.

The authors report versatility across tasks, objectives, behaviors, and different robot manipulators. They also report successful generalization to unseen tasks using a few demonstrations. Although the paper opens with the possibility of prompting from one demonstration, its stated generalization finding concerns few-shot inputs. Beyond simulation, the authors directly deploy generated policies on real robots for locomotion tasks, extending the evaluation to physical execution.
neurips-2024-make-an-agent-a-generalizab.tldr: Make-An-Agent uses behavior-conditioned diffusion to generate policy networks, with few-shot generalization and real-robot locomotion demonstrations.

paragraphs: OlympicArena is a benchmark for evaluating demanding reasoning in language and multimodal models. It contains 11,163 bilingual problems spanning seven fields and 62 international Olympiad competitions. Problems include both text-only material and combinations of text and images. The authors examine the dataset rigorously for data leakage to support meaningful assessment of model performance.

The evaluation goes beyond checking final answers. It studies performance across disciplines and modalities, and examines reasoning processes in problems with lengthy solutions. This broader view matters because a model’s overall answer accuracy does not by itself describe how it handles extended reasoning or integrates information from images with text.

In the reported evaluation, GPT-4o achieves 39.97% overall accuracy, with 28.67% in mathematics and 29.71% in physics. These results illustrate substantial remaining difficulty on the benchmark’s complex reasoning tasks. The project also supplies an annotation platform, evaluation tooling, and a leaderboard with automatic submissions. Together, these resources provide a structured way to measure progress on challenging multidisciplinary problems.
neurips-2024-olympicarena-benchmarking-m.tldr: OlympicArena evaluates multidisciplinary text-and-image reasoning through 11,163 competition problems and reveals substantial difficulties for the tested models.

paragraphs: OpenGaussian extends open-vocabulary understanding to individual 3D points in scenes represented with 3D Gaussian Splatting. The authors observe that existing methods mainly parse two-dimensional pixels and struggle with point-level tasks. They identify weak feature representations and inaccurate links between 2D and 3D features as central obstacles to understanding objects directly in the 3D representation.

The method first trains instance features using SAM masks without cross-frame mask associations. The resulting features aim to remain consistent within an object while distinguishing different objects in 3D. A two-stage codebook then discretizes them: a coarse stage uses point positions for location-based clustering, followed by a finer refinement stage.

Finally, an instance-level association mechanism links 3D points to 2D masks and connects those masks to CLIP features. This supplies the connection needed for open-vocabulary understanding at the point level. Experiments cover language-based 3D object selection, point-cloud understanding, and click-based selection, alongside ablation studies. The reported results support the effectiveness of the combined representation and association pipeline across these tasks.
neurips-2024-opengaussian-towards-point-.tldr: OpenGaussian combines consistent instance features, hierarchical discretization, and 2D–3D associations to support open-vocabulary understanding of 3D points.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many members of a coalition should enter each of a sequence of second-price auctions. A decision-maker has limited observations, while agents draw their values from an unknown distribution. The objective is to maximize the coalition’s cumulative reward as its selected members compete with a fixed number of outside agents.

The authors model each possible number of participating coalition members as an arm in a structured bandit problem. Their Local-Greedy and Greedy-Grid algorithms exploit relationships between these choices: feedback from one arm can estimate rewards for others. The analysis combines these estimates, concentration bounds within suitable neighborhoods, and a reward-unimodality property that holds under standard assumptions on the value distribution.

Both algorithms achieve constant problem-dependent regret under the stated framework. Greedy-Grid also has problem-independent guarantees. In practical comparisons, however, Local-Greedy performs better than Greedy-Grid and the tested standard bandit methods, avoiding reliance on confidence intervals. The results distinguish strong theoretical guarantees from observed performance and show how auction structure can make limited feedback useful across participation choices.
neurips-2024-optimizing-the-coalition-ga.tldr: Two structured-bandit algorithms learn coalition participation levels in repeated auctions, achieving constant problem-dependent regret under the stated assumptions.

paragraphs: PaGoDA addresses the computational expense of diffusion-based content generation, particularly during training. Its central idea is to train the diffusion component on lower-resolution data and use a staged process to obtain a generator capable of producing higher-resolution outputs. This connects cheaper diffusion training with single-step generation at inference.

The pipeline has three stages: train diffusion on downsampled data, distill the pretrained diffusion model, and progressively increase resolution through super-resolution. The authors report a 64-fold reduction in the cost of training the diffusion model when using eightfold-downsampled data. That figure describes the diffusion-training component, so its meaning is tied to where the pipeline reduces the resolution.

The resulting single-step generator reportedly reaches state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet at resolutions from 64 by 64 through 512 by 512, and in text-to-image generation. The pipeline can also operate in latent space, adding compression alongside an existing latent-diffusion autoencoder. These findings present progressive growth as a way to connect a low-resolution diffusion teacher to efficient generation across multiple output resolutions.
neurips-2024-pagoda-progressive-growing-.tldr: PaGoDA distills a low-resolution diffusion teacher and progressively increases resolution to produce a competitive single-step generator.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether knowledge already written in tutorial books can be turned into a policy network. The motivation is that learning decision-making skills commonly requires many interactions with an environment, even when relevant guidance is available in text. The authors define Policy Learning from tutorial Books as a way to use that existing knowledge through language-model systems.

Their Understanding, Rehearsing, and Introspecting framework follows three stages. It first derives knowledge from the books, then rehearses decision-making trajectories based on that understanding. Finally, it uses introspection within the resulting imaginary dataset to distill a policy network. The training material for the policy therefore comes from rehearsed trajectories grounded in the written guidance.

The authors construct benchmarks based on Tic-Tac-Toe and Football. They report at least a 44% net win rate against GPT-based agents without real data. In Football, their policy wins against built-in AI opponents at a 37% rate, compared with 6% for a GPT-based agent. These results support the feasibility of converting textual instruction into effective policies in the studied games.
neurips-2024-policy-learning-from-tutori.tldr: A three-stage framework turns tutorial-book knowledge into imagined trajectories and then policy networks, showing effective game play without real training data.

paragraphs: Optimal transport provides ways to realign datasets, either through a matrix describing how mass moves between points or through a map that moves points directly. Entropic optimal transport is widely useful, but its regularization strength is difficult to tune. The same parameter affects computational speed, statistical behavior, generalization, and bias, creating several interacting design considerations.

ProgOT divides the overall displacement into a sequence of smaller steps inspired by dynamic optimal transport. Each step is solved with entropic optimal transport using appropriately scheduled parameters. This progressive formulation can estimate both transport plans and transport maps, distributing the work of alignment across time-discretized stages instead of treating displacement as one operation.

Experiments show that ProgOT computes large-scale couplings faster and more robustly than standard solvers, including outperforming the evaluated neural-network approaches. The paper also proves statistical consistency for its transport-map estimates. These are complementary findings: the experiments establish practical advantages in the tested computations, while the consistency result supplies a theoretical foundation for the map-estimation approach.
neurips-2024-progressive-entropic-optima.tldr: ProgOT solves transport progressively with scheduled entropic parameters, improving large-scale coupling computation and providing consistent transport-map estimates.

paragraphs: Proportionally fair clustering gives stronger group-fairness protections to groups that are larger and more cohesive. Earlier work measured each point’s clustering cost through its distance to an assigned center. This paper extends the framework to settings where clusters have no required centers, and a point’s cost depends on the other points placed with it.

The authors consider several cost functions, including both metric and non-metric ones. They show that Greedy Capture, an algorithm originally developed for centroid-based clustering, still provides strong proportional-fairness guarantees in this broader setting. The guarantees differ substantially from the earlier ones and require new proof techniques. They also introduce algorithms for auditing the fairness of an existing clustering.

Experiments on real data suggest that traditional clustering algorithms can be highly unfair under this framework. The proposed algorithms achieve strong fairness guarantees with a moderate loss in common clustering objectives in those experiments. The work therefore supplies both methods for constructing fairer clusters and tools for assessing whether a given grouping respects the framework’s group-level protections.
neurips-2024-proportional-fairness-in-no.tldr: Proportional-fairness guarantees and auditing algorithms are extended to clustering defined by relationships among members rather than assigned centers.

paragraphs: This paper revisits few-shot object detection in light of vision-language models pretrained on web-scale data. The authors report that GroundingDINO’s zero-shot predictions substantially outperform state-of-the-art few-shot detectors on COCO, at 48 versus 33 AP. This motivates reconsidering what a handful of labeled examples should accomplish when a model already has broad recognition capabilities.

They propose treating few-shot recognition as alignment to a target application’s concepts. For example, an application’s definition of a truck may differ from the category learned from web data. Examples can therefore combine text with visual cues, resembling the instructions used to explain a labeling task to human annotators.

The resulting Foundational FSOD protocol permits pretraining on any external data and evaluates adaptation using multimodal K-shot examples for each target class. The authors repurpose nuImages, benchmark open-source vision-language models, and analyze existing methods. They also report that their competition’s winning entry exceeds their baseline by 23.3 mAP, demonstrating substantial gains under the proposed concept-alignment evaluation.
neurips-2024-revisiting-few-shot-object-.tldr: Foundational FSOD reframes few-shot detection as adapting pretrained vision-language models to application-specific concepts using text and visual examples.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits repeatedly choose among candidate actions using available context and the rewards observed from earlier choices. Neural versions use expressive networks to model these decisions, but corrupted reward labels can mislead learning. This paper targets adversarial reward corruption, where the feedback used to judge actions can drive unexpected degradation in the learner’s performance.

The proposed R-NeuralUCB algorithm introduces a context-aware gradient-descent training strategy to improve robustness. Its core intervention concerns how the neural model learns from reward feedback in relation to context. The aim is to retain the representational benefits of neural bandits while making their learning process more resistant to corrupted observations.

The authors provide a regret analysis under an overparameterized neural-network setting, quantifying the effect of reward corruption on performance. Their analysis avoids the arm-separateness assumption commonly used in prior neural-bandit work, while retaining the stated network-setting assumption. Experiments compare R-NeuralUCB with baselines on real datasets under different scenarios and support its effectiveness. Together, the analysis and experiments address both the measurable consequences of corruption and a training strategy for reducing them.
neurips-2024-robust-neural-contextual-ba.tldr: R-NeuralUCB uses context-aware training to improve resistance to corrupted rewards, with regret guarantees for overparameterized networks and supporting experiments.

paragraphs: ShareGPT4Video develops detailed video captions to improve both video understanding and text-to-video generation. The authors find that straightforward ways of feeding multiple frames to GPT4V can miss detail and confuse temporal relationships. They identify three needs: accurately describing changes between frames, preserving detail within frames, and scaling the number of frames to accommodate different video lengths.

Their differential captioning strategy supports videos of varied resolutions, aspect ratios, and lengths. It produces a dataset of 40,000 videos with dense GPT4V annotations covering object attributes, camera movement, world knowledge, and detailed event timing. This dataset then supports training ShareCaptioner-Video, an efficient captioning model used to annotate another 4.8 million aesthetically appealing videos.

The authors validate those larger-scale annotations on a ten-second text-to-video generation task. For understanding, they test the caption dataset across several video-language architectures and introduce ShareGPT4Video-8B, reporting state-of-the-art results on three video benchmarks. The series connects a carefully designed annotation strategy to a scalable captioner and downstream evidence that richer video descriptions benefit both understanding and generation.
neurips-2024-sharegpt4video-improving-vi.tldr: ShareGPT4Video combines detailed temporal captioning, large-scale annotations, and video models to improve video understanding and text-to-video generation.

paragraphs: Scattered Online Inference addresses neural-network computation on small microcontrollers, especially where predictions must arrive quickly. The paper notes that increased processing power has still left the smallest appliances unable to run even moderately large state-of-the-art networks in time-sensitive settings. Its approach seeks to reduce the work required for repeated inference on time-series inputs.

SOI uses continuity and seasonality in the input data and model predictions to support extrapolation. Rather than fully recalculating the network at every inference, it estimates parts of the model’s internal state. The abstract highlights deeper layers as a particular opportunity for processing-speed improvements through this use of temporal structure.

Compression produces more general internal partial states that enable this selective recalculation. The central idea is therefore to exploit relationships across successive inputs and predictions, allowing some internal computation to be estimated. The approach’s motivation is tied to the continuity and seasonality described in the abstract. Its stated contribution is a method for reducing computational complexity through partial-state estimation in repeated inference.
neurips-2024-soi-scaling-down-computatio.tldr: SOI exploits temporal continuity and seasonality to estimate internal neural-network states and avoid full recalculation at every inference.

paragraphs: Pretrained diffusion models can supply internal features for discriminative tasks as well as generate images. This paper identifies a problem called content shift: the content represented by those features can differ from the input image, including differences in an object’s exact shape. The authors attribute the phenomenon to an inherent characteristic of diffusion models, suggesting it is broadly present.

Their empirical analysis finds that content shift can harm performance even when the discrepancy is not visually apparent. They connect it to information drift during recovery of an image from noisy input. That connection suggests using existing image-generation techniques to suppress the drift and improve the fidelity of features used for discrimination.

The authors introduce GATE, a practical guideline for efficiently assessing whether a generation technique is likely to help, and provide an implementation of the approach. They report superior results across multiple tasks and datasets despite the method’s simplicity. These results support content-shift suppression as a potentially general way to improve diffusion features, connecting the quality of image recovery to the usefulness of internal representations.
neurips-2024-suppress-content-shift-bett.tldr: Suppressing content drift with existing generation techniques improves diffusion-model features for discriminative tasks across the tested settings.

paragraphs: WaterMax is a watermarking scheme for text generated by large language models. The paper focuses on obtaining a watermark that is easy to detect while preserving the original model’s text quality. This matters because the authors describe existing watermarking approaches as facing a trade-off in which greater robustness comes at the expense of generated-text quality.

The design leaves the language model itself untouched: it changes neither model weights, output logits, nor temperature. The authors instead frame WaterMax’s central balance as one between robustness and computational complexity. This shifts the design consideration toward the computation needed to obtain robust watermarking while sustaining the quality of the underlying generator.

The paper reports both theoretical support and experimental validation for its performance. It also reports outperforming the compared state-of-the-art techniques across its benchmark suite. Taken together, the stated findings support the possibility of combining high detectability with preserved generation quality through this design. The remaining balance highlighted in the abstract concerns computational complexity and robustness, making computational cost an explicit part of the method’s approach.
neurips-2024-watermax-breaking-the-llm-w.tldr: WaterMax reports highly detectable text watermarks while preserving language-model output quality, balancing robustness against computational complexity.
